# ADR-0020: Use camelCase JSON contracts with TypeScript bindings generated by ts-rs

**Status:** Accepted  
**Date:** 2026-10-31  
**Deciders:** Architect, by delegation from the product owner  
**Affects:** TRD §6.1, §11; ADR-0002, ADR-0003, ADR-0005; [engineering standards §3.1 and §3.3](../ENGINEERING-STANDARDS.md#33-contracts-and-schemas); [coding standards §2.2](../CODING-STANDARDS.md#22-cross-cutting-names)  
**Revisit trigger:** a stable (non-prerelease) `specta`/`tauri-specta` 2.x release that also generates command bindings, or ts-rs failing to express a contract type the API needs.

## Context

ADR-0003 requires TypeScript bindings generated from the Rust API types and validation at the process boundary, but did not fix the JSON field casing or the generator. Rust fields are `snake_case`; TypeScript properties are `camelCase`; the desktop client's hand-written types (`apps/desktop/src/api/types.ts`) already use camelCase and discriminated unions with a `kind` tag. The engineering standards named a `schema_version` field, written before the UI language was chosen. Two casings on one contract would force a mapping layer or a second, hand-maintained mirror of every type, which the coding standards forbid.

## Decision

1. **Casing:** every JSON contract (Tauri commands and channels, the local IPC API of ADR-0002, persisted JSON, exported files, and generated JSON Schemas) uses **camelCase** field names, produced by `#[serde(rename_all = "camelCase")]` on contract types. The version field is `schemaVersion`. Enum variants serialize as an internally tagged union with a `kind` field whose values are kebab-case (`#[serde(tag = "kind", rename_all = "kebab-case")]`). SQL tables and columns stay `snake_case` (ADR-0005).
2. **Bindings:** TypeScript types are generated from the Rust contract crate (`onecode-api`) with **ts-rs** (12.x line, the newest stable release ≥14 days old at adoption). Generated files live in `apps/desktop/src/api/generated/`, are committed, carry a "generated, do not edit" header, and a CI check fails if regeneration changes them. The current hand-written `types.ts` is replaced by re-exports from the generated files when `onecode-api` exists.
3. **Schemas:** `schemars` generates JSON Schemas for the same types into `schemas/`, with golden tests (engineering standards §3.1).
4. **Validation:** the Rust side validates every inbound payload by strict deserialization plus schema-level limits (size, depth, string length) before any handler runs. The UI treats the core as the trusted producer but still checks the `schemaVersion` major, enforces payload size limits on channels, handles unknown `kind` values through an exhaustive `switch` with a safe default, and renders any untrusted content inside a payload as text (secure coding §5).

## Alternatives considered

| Option | Summary | Why not (or why not yet) |
|---|---|---|
| snake_case on the wire | Matches Rust field names directly | Forces snake_case property access throughout the React code or a mapping layer; conflicts with the existing client types |
| `specta` + `tauri-specta` | Generates types and typed command wrappers | Only release candidates for 2.x on 2026-10-31; the dependency policy admits stable releases only |
| Hand-written TypeScript mirrors | No generator | Two sources of truth that drift; forbidden by coding standards §1.3 |
| Runtime schema validation in the UI (e.g., Ajv) | Validate every core message in the browser | The core is the trusted producer in the same app; the cost and bundle size buy little over version, size, and exhaustiveness checks |

## Consequences

- **Positive:** one contract definition in Rust; idiomatic TypeScript; breaking changes surface as compile errors in the UI.
- **Negative and mitigations:** ts-rs does not generate command wrappers, so `src/api/` keeps a thin typed wrapper per command, reviewed with the contract; serde attributes must be applied consistently, enforced by a unit test that round-trips every contract type and checks casing.
- **Platform differences:** none.
- **Migration or rollback path:** generated files are plain TypeScript; switching to another generator replaces the generation step without changing call sites.

## Threat model

| Asset | Entry point | Trust level of input | Abuse case | Mitigation | Test |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Core handlers | Tauri commands and IPC requests | UI or local client: untrusted for authorization | Malformed, oversized, or extra-field payloads reach handlers | Strict serde deserialization, size/depth limits, server-side policy | Fuzz and malformed-payload tests per command |
| UI state | Channel events | Core-produced; may embed repository content | Version-mismatched or oversized events, embedded markup | `schemaVersion` check, size limits, exhaustive `kind` handling, text rendering | Version-mismatch and XSS fixtures |

## Verification

- Round-trip test for every contract type asserting camelCase keys and kebab-case `kind` values.
- CI step regenerates bindings and schemas and fails on any diff.
- `npm run typecheck` in `apps/desktop` compiles against the generated types.
